key: NAUGHT is to-day, to-morrow naught. Who comprehends the mystery? We must address ourselves unto another’s thought, and lost is then the hope we formed.
s: A short hymn of quarrel over an offering, naming Indra, Agastya and the Maruts, opens with a complaint; Sāyaṇa, on 1.170.1, hears Indra lamenting an offering set aside for him and given to another, and giving up hope of it today or tomorrow.

evidence.gloss: The manner of the lament is set out. Indra says: what belongs to today, that is not ours today ... nor tomorrow either. The sense is: as today what was set aside for us is not ours, how will it be obtained tomorrow? “What is strange”: the reversal, that having been set aside for one it is given to another, who knows that? Or: who knows what is to come? It is thus said that the hope that it will be obtained today or tomorrow should not be held.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref 1.170.1, at [169,1]). Sāyaṇa on 1.170.1 opens ‘the manner of the lament is set out; Indra says’, glosses the verse as what was set aside for us (asmadartha-nirupta) is not ours today, so how tomorrow, takes ‘the mystery’ as the reversal of an offering set aside for one and given to another, and concludes that hope of getting it today or tomorrow should not be held; the hymn introduction quotes Yāska on Agastya setting aside an oblation for Indra and wishing to give it to the Maruts, and Wilson’s note agrees. Plain sense faithful: verses 2 to 5 name the Maruts, Agastya and Indra and argue over oblations; no four-word overlap. Source year confirmed by the Wikisource API (2019-07-27). entry-check ok.
